title: AI agents are coming to Rivian’s cars
summary: Rivian recently rolled out an AI assistant that lets drivers and passengers interact with the company’s electric vehicles just by talking to them. Scaringe didn’t say when Rivian would implement this, and the company declined to offer more details, pointing instead to the “AI & Autonomy Day” event it’s hosting in December. But it’s not hard to imagine how Rivian might integrate something like Claude, OpenAI’s Dots, or Meta’s Muse assistant into its software. Of course, Rivian wouldn’t be the first American car company to add AI agents to a car’s software. title: Google’s Universal Cart shopping tool launches in the US
summary: Google on Thursday said “Universal Cart,” a tool that lets users collect and monitor products they find across search and in the Gemini app, is now available to U.S. users. The company first previewed the tool at Google I/O in May. UCP is designed to help AI agents and retailers work together across different parts of the shopping journey, including checkout. Google is already deeply invested in AI-powered shopping, and Universal Cart is its latest effort to make the experience more convenient. It joins features such as conversational product discovery in Search’s AI Mode and Google’s “Let Google Call” tool, which uses an AI agent to contact nearby stores and check whether an item is in stock. Amazon , OpenAI , and other rivals have added agentic commerce features as companies look for ways to make chatbots useful beyond answering questions.

title: CopilotKit Releases CLiF: A Continual Learning Platform That Turns Agent Traces and User Actions into Skills, Evals, and Fine-Tuning Data
summary: CopilotKit, the company behind the open-source CopilotKit framework and the AG-UI protocol, released CLiF , a platform for continual learning from full-stack trajectories, in early access . CLiF securely captures what the agent does and what users do in the product, and turns that record into skills, production-based evals, and fine-tuning datasets, all exportable along with the raw trajectories. CopilotKit’s view, laid out in its explainer on agent learning , is that how users actually get work done is the most valuable dataset any agent team has, and that it is rarely captured in a form an agent can learn from. For any other agent or MCP server, skills can be downloaded as plain files with copilotkit skills download <container> –output <dir>. On the agent side, CLiF builds on Automatic Learning , the capability in CopilotKit Intelligence that CopilotKit also positions as the foundation for self-improving agents .

title: An OpenAI Employee Allegedly Used a Chatbot to Help Plant a Recording Device at the Office
summary: An engineer at OpenAI allegedly concealed an audio recording device in a piece of toilet paper and attached it behind a monitor inside an executive conference room at one of the company’s San Francisco offices, based on a criminal complaint unsealed on Tuesday. He also appears to have used a chatbot account associated with his spouse to ask various technical questions about setting up a covert audio recording device, based on prosecutors and the court filing. OpenAI’s security team also allegedly found an additional recording device in Alfozan’s bag at the office. According to the complaint, Alfozan allegedly planted the listening device “no later than on or about September 28, 2026.” The conference room Alfozan targeted “can be reserved only by executives and executive assistants,” and is typically used “for internal leadership meetings,” “technical and product sessions,” and “external briefings” with business partners and government officials, based on the complaint.

title: OpenAI employee arrested for allegedly planting a bug in a conference room
summary: The recording device was apparently discovered plugged into a TV’s USB port in an executive meeting room. An OpenAI engineer was arrested after the company noted it discovered a “sophisticated recording device” hidden in one of its offices. OpenAI’s post about the incident says it used its AI models to “understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier.” As noted by the DOJ, OpenAI found the device plugged into a TV’s USB port in an executive conference room, where discussions about “highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information” often take place. title: Judge orders OpenAI to turn over hiring records in Apple trade secrets case
summary: A judge has ruled that Apple will gain expedited access to OpenAI’s hiring materials in the trade secrets-focused lawsuit the iPhone maker filed against OpenAI in July. Specifically, the court will allow Apple to view documents associated with OpenAI’s interviews with former Apple employees who applied for roles within its consumer hardware and robotics groups ahead of the rumored launch of OpenAI’s first hardware device. The court gave OpenAI five days to turn over materials it has already collected and 14 days for any other materials related to this request, agreeing with Apple that these documents should be expedited. U.S. District Judge Edward Davila didn’t greenlight all of Apple’s requests for expedited access to OpenAI documents and messages relevant to the case. But he did rule that Apple could access the interview materials, alongside private LINE messages (from a messaging app) between individuals named in the case, including OpenAI employees Chang Liu and Alyssa Peng.

summary: Representatives for OpenAI and Anthropic told a British parliamentary hearing that voluntary pledges were no longer enough to ensure safety and that new laws should be introduced, deepening a public schism with Google DeepMind and Meta , both of which declined to back new legislation. The Business, Innovation, Science, and Trade Committee, comprising a cross-party panel of MPs, held an evidence session on Tuesday with appearances from four frontier AI firms, four former staff of the firms turned whistleblowers and senior British civil servants. “The rules should be binding,” Anthropic’s head of Europe Liam Booth-Smith told the committee, when asked if the company’s view was that AI safety now needs a statutory framework .

title: Facebook is giving users more control over their algorithm
summary: Facebook is the latest social media platform to give users greater control over the algorithm that determines what appears in their feeds. The new tool allows Facebook users to influence the content they see in Feed and Reels by describing their preferences in their own words using natural language. Users can adjust their preferences and interact with the algorithms responsible for ranking and recommending posts, with changes reflected in their recommendations in real time. The company has also updated Facebook’s three-dot menu, making it easier for users to manage their content preferences directly from individual posts. By opening the menu, users can access “Your Algorithm” or select the “Interested” and “Not interested” options to indicate whether particular content aligns with their preferences. Users can explain what they want to see more or less of, helping Facebook refine its recommendations based on their responses.

title: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world
summary: If there’s one lesson the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident taught us, it’s that AI agents can be unpredictable. “Imagine if something like that happened in the physical world,” Howie Sun, CEO and co-founder of Laplace Intelligence , told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real world, and we don’t really want physical AI to fail in the real world.” Ann Arbor-based Laplace is building automated red-teaming — essentially, stress-testing a system by deliberately trying to make it fail — for robotics and physical AI. That’s when the calls started coming in from autonomous vehicle companies interested in implementing their ideas. “I realized that I wanted to build this and take it from purely academic research into a product that’s useful in the real world,” Sun said. At the startup’s core is a high-fidelity simulation reconstructed from the real world, paired with an AI agent that constantly probes for weaknesses and failure points.

summary: Personal AI agents are increasingly making transactions on their users’ behalf, but given the nondeterministic nature of large language models, AI bots are prone to doing what they’re not supposed to. title: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
summary: Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs. There’s the autonomous hack that OpenAI agents executed against Hugging Face in July, but human misuse is a real threat too: According to a recent risk report from Anthropic , several extensive hacking operations have been undertaken with the assistance of Claude. After it was hacked by OpenAI agents, Hugging Face emphasized the fact that it had to depend on an open model to analyze the hack, because questions about it triggered the closed models’ security filters. The OpenAI Hugging Face hack only occurred because the company’s models were being tested with many of their cybersecurity guardrails removed, and open models have very few guardrails in the first place. If the risks of open models are less black-and-white than they might at first seem, so are the benefits.

title: Microsoft president says UK is best placed to drive AI regulation
summary: Microsoft president Brad Smith is calling for urgent regulation of AI, and his argument is that consumer products like milk and washing machines have more oversight than the companies building artificial intelligence. Smith also said the U.K., and not the U.S. or European Union, is best placed to lead on global safety rules. Last month, he reportedly asked Anthropic and OpenAI to withhold new models from British testers, but AISI confirmed on Monday that it is able to access and test the latest models. Despite the president’s pushback, however, Smith argued the U.K. can regulate AI in ways that the U.S. cannot. “In Washington, D.C., people don’t look at the U.K. and they don’t look at London the way they look at Brussels,” he told the BBC. “That’s a strength.” His comments come amid rallying cries from tech leaders, including Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, to slow the pace of AI development in the wake of several incidents where AI agents went rogue.
